headline: Maine's Alewife Fish Make Stunning Comeback After Dam Removals
meta_description: Maine's alewife population surged from fewer than 800 to over 9 million in 35 years thanks to dam removals and fish passage projects.
summary_short: Dam removals and fish passage projects in Maine have restored alewife migration routes, allowing the population to explode from 800 to 9 million fish.
body:
Maine's alewife fish population has experienced a remarkable resurgence, climbing from fewer than 800 to more than 9 million individuals over the past 35 years. This dramatic recovery demonstrates how removing barriers to natural migration can restore entire ecosystems.

The turnaround stems from targeted infrastructure projects designed to reopen pathways that alewives need to complete their life cycle. Dam removals and fish passage installations have allowed the species to migrate freely once again, reconnecting fragmented populations and enabling breeding patterns that had been disrupted for decades.

The story of Maine's alewife represents a broader lesson in conservation: sometimes restoring nature requires stepping back and undoing human obstacles rather than imposing new solutions. By prioritizing the fish's own needs—access to their ancestral waterways—Maine has achieved what many thought impossible: a return to abundance.
quick_facts: Alewife population grew from under 800 to over 9 million in 35 years
Dam removals and fish passage projects restored migration routes in Maine
Species recovery driven by removing barriers to natural fish movement
